lesson.title_tag: Stephanie -- Lesson 03 -- The Scene and the Verdict
lesson.grammar_point: past continuous x past simple por função narrativa; modais de recomendação
lesson._phases: As 8 etapas do framework grammar-for-communication, contrato v1. Somam 55: 6+5+9+7+7+8+9+4.

items: What you watched
Two weeks ago you sat at the back of a class. Three things happened, and you have to describe them to the teacher tomorrow.
The catch
Describing is not judging. Today the difference is not politeness — it is which words you use.

diag_attempt.title: Describe each moment. One sentence. The way it comes out today.
items: The students were in pairs. You walked around. The back table went quiet when you got there.
Say what you saw — not what it means.
The instruction was given while the students were still writing.
Same rule: the moment, not the verdict.
Two students finished early and sat doing nothing for four minutes.
Same rule.

diag_attempt.label: Four minutes. No help, no phrases — this is the part I need to hear.

disc_sort.title: Six lines from a report. Sort each one by what it does for the reader.
cols: Paints the scene — you are in the room
States what happened — a fact with edges
Judges it — a verdict, not a description
items: The students were working in pairs.
The back table went quiet.
The pair work did not work.
They were still writing when you started talking.
Two of them finished four minutes early.
The instructions were unclear.

disc_analyse.title: Look at the first two groups. Both are true, and both are past.
items: Which one puts the teacher back in the room, watching?
Which one could go straight into a report, with a full stop after it?
What changes in the VERBS — not in the tone?

disc_answer.title: Reveal what changes
list: SCENE = were + -ing. It was in progress; it has no edges; you are inside it looking around.
EVENT = past simple. It happened and it finished. It has edges, so it can be counted, dated, quoted.
VERDICT = neither. 'Did not work' and 'unclear' are conclusions with no moment attached — and a conclusion is something he can argue with before he has pictured anything.
So the order is not a style choice: scene, then event, then — only then — what you would try.
disc_answer.note: This is the whole lesson. Everything after is practice.

clar.title: The three jobs, and the form that does each
cards: In progress, no edges. 'They were working in pairs.' Puts him back in the room.
Finished, with edges. 'The back table went quiet.' Can be dated and quoted.
Not past at all — and that is the point. 'You might try…' is the only one he can refuse.

clar.text: when + past simple cuts into the scene. while + were -ing holds it open.

clar_reveal.title: Two lines that sound the same and land differently
clar_reveal.sub: Read each pair out loud. Say which one you would rather receive, then click.
items: “When you gave the instruction, they wrote.” / “When you gave the instruction, they were still writing.”
The first says they started writing because of you — which is not what happened. The second says the writing was already running when the instruction landed on top of it. Same event, opposite cause.
essencial
“The activity did not work.” / “The back table stopped talking after four minutes.”
The first he can only accept or fight. The second he can picture — and then decide for himself whether it worked.
essencial
“You have to give the instruction first.” / “One thing you might try is giving it first.”
Same content, and only one of them leaves him a reply. This is the line from Lesson 1 — the form changed, the job did not.
condicional

parts: the instruction again while the others

pers_case.title: Three moments from a class YOU watched this term.
items: One moment where something was already happening when the teacher did something.
were + -ing, then past simple.
One moment that finished, with edges.
past simple. Give it a time if you can.
One thing you would try — and he can refuse.
might / could. Not 'you have to'.

pers_evi.title: Before you say it: what makes each one describable?
items: A scene is describable if you could have filmed it.
“They were working in pairs” — a camera would show it. “They were engaged” — it would not.
An event is describable if it has a moment.
“The back table went quiet” has one. “The activity failed” has none.
A suggestion is describable if he can say no to it.
“You might try…” he can. “You have to…” he cannot.
Your side
Your colleague watched a class and sends you five notes — short, and not always complete. You turn each one into something the teacher can use.
The catch
Some notes are already a verdict. Those you cannot report as they are: you have to ask what was actually seen before you pass them on.

task_brief.label: Take these in. Keywords, not sentences.
items: were + -ing for the scene
past simple for the event
might / could for what to try
What did you actually see?

wb.title: How it went
campos: Verdict that slipped through (for the checkpoint)

retask.title: Say only the note your teacher marked — once more.
items: Same moment. What changes is whether he can picture it before he judges it.

fecho.title: What we built today
items: The scene is were + -ing: no edges, and he is back in the room.
The event is past simple: it has edges, so it can be dated and quoted.
A verdict is neither — it is a conclusion with no moment attached.
Ask what was seen before you pass on someone else's verdict.

fecho.title: How confident do you feel right now?
fecho.sub: Your own reading, today. There is no right answer here.
items: Describing a moment so the other person can picture it
Saying what happened without saying what it means
Noticing when what I am about to say is already a verdict
Asking a colleague what they actually saw
